Senses.PreferredTarget: a general address to the community
Senses.Explanation: Literally broad or general speaking, this names the Chan institution of a general address to the community and, in verbal grammar, delivering that same address. The Classified Essentials of the Patriarchs lists “ascending the hall, small gathering, address to the assembly, and general address” (上堂、小參、示眾、普說) as separate headings. The monastic code makes its organization explicit: a general-address placard is hung before the monks' hall and common quarters, a venue is prepared, and the drum is sounded after gruel. Records qualify an address by occasion, as in an “incident-related general address” (因事普說), and record masters being requested to give one after questioning or before the summer retreat. A speaker can say, “I will give you all one general address” (為諸人普說一上), while another request specifies the subject with “give a general address on this” (普說此). The ordinary wording is thus institutionalized as a placarded public recorded-sayings genre with venue, occasion, audience, and questioning. Event, heading, and delivery are grammatical presentations of the same institution, not different lexical things.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 870 hits in 134 texts. Noun and verb constructions denote the same general-address event; the two former targets could not distinguish different referents without their explanations and are merged. The general-address placard (普說牌) names the placard for this genre, not another sense. General address remains distinct from ascending the hall (上堂), small gathering (小參), addressing the assembly (示眾), question-and-answer (問答), and taking up the whisk (秉拂).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a 'general invitation' or 'summons to all'; in the Chan corpus it is the organized call for the community's shared labor. The term occurs 1,567 times in 282 allowed texts. The monastic regulations define it directly: 'the rule of the general work summons is that upper and lower share the labor equally' (普請之法蓋上下均力也). The same section says that when work requires the assembly's combined strength, the administrators report it, inform the head monk and disciplinarian, and hang the general-summons placard (報眾掛普請牌); at the wooden-fish or drum signal, those not exempted go together to the work site. Encounter records name the labor. Baizhang returns from a summons to open fields and Huangbo calls it 'the assembly monks doing work' (普請開田；眾僧作務). Nanquan asks the disciplinarian what today's summons will do and receives the answer 'pull the mill' (今日普請作甚麼。對曰。拽磨). Dongshan inspects the quarters during a summons and finds a monk who did not attend. A lamp record places a monk hoeing during the summons when the meal drum sounds, and another records a summons to pick tea (普請摘茶). Other recurrent activities include hoeing, sorting vegetables or bracken, carrying firewood, planting rice, and planting trees. The word names the all-community summons and its work.
Senses.Note: The direct regulations definition is supported by early lamp and encounter records. 'During the general work summons' (普請次) occurs 96 times in 51 texts; 'attend the general work summons' (赴普請) occurs nine times in nine texts; and 'go out for the general work summons' (出普請) occurs six times in five texts. No competing self-definition was found. Figurative invitations to the assembly to look are deployment extensions, not a separate sense.
